ἔζευξεν ἄνθρωπος μὴ χωριζέτω. σύμφωνα δὲ καὶ ταῦτα, τὸ ἐὰν δὲ καὶ χωρισθῇ,
μενέτω ἄγαμος τοῖς εἰρημένοις τῷ κυρίῳ ἐὰν ἀπολελυμένην τις γαμήσῃ, μοιχᾶται
κἀκείνη ἐὰν γαμηθῇ ἄλλῳ. 1 Kor 7,12 Οὐχ ὡς ἀντινομοθετῶν λέγει· ἐγώ, οὐχ ὁ
κύριος, ἀλλ' ὅτι τινὰ μὲν δι' ἑαυτοῦ εἶπεν ὁ κύριος, τινὰ δὲ νῦν πρῶτον εἴρηται παρὰ
τοῦ ἀποστόλου περὶ τῆς διαστάσεως τοῦ ἀπίστου, καὶ διδάσκει ὅτι οὐχ ἡ ἀπιστία
κρατεῖ τῆς πίστεως, ἀλλ' ἡ πίστις τοῦ συνόντος ἁγιάζει καὶ τὸν ἄπιστον. 1 Kor 7,13
Οὐ τὸ λαμβάνειν ἄπιστόν φησιν, ἀλλὰ τὸ ἀνέχεσθαι ἀπίστου. 1 Kor 7,14 Ἅγιά ἐστι τὰ
τέκνα καθαρὰ καὶ οὐ μεμολυσμένα καὶ ὑπὸ τῆς ἀπιστίας· νικᾷ γὰρ ἐπ' αὐτῶν ἡ πίστις
τῶν γονέων ἤπερ ἡ ἀπιστία. 1 Kor 7,17 Τῷ μὲν ἐμέρισεν ὁ θεὸς τὸ σῶσαι, τῷ δὲ
σωθῆναι, ἑκάστῳ ἀπονείμας τὸ ἐπάξιον αὐτοῦ. τὸ δὲ ἑκάστῳ ὡς ἐμέρισεν ὁ θεὸς οὐ
τὸ ἔχειν ἄπιστόν φησιν, ἀλλὰ τὸ ἀνέχεσθαι ἀπίστου. 251,ξολ2 1 Kor 7,18–24 Οὐ δι'
ἑαυτὴν ἡ περιτομὴ καλή, ἀλλ' ὅτι ἐντολὴ θεοῦ, καὶ ἡ ἀκροβυστία δημιουργία θεοῦ,
οὐ μισθὸς τῶν ἀκροβύστων. εἶτά φησι περὶ τοῦ δούλου· μὴ σπουδάσῃς περὶ τὴν
πρόσκαιρον ἐλευθερίαν, ἀλλ' εἰ καὶ δύνασαι, μᾶλλον χρῆσαι τῇ δουλείᾳ· μείζων γὰρ
ὁ μισθός, ὅταν καὶ περὶ τὴν τῶν ἀνθρώπων δουλείαν ἠσχολημένος οὐκ ἀμελεῖ τοῦ
εὐαρεστῆσαι θεῷ. ἕκαστος δὲ ἐν ᾧ ἐκλήθη μενέτω, καὶ δοῦλος ἐπὶ τῇ δουλείᾳ μὴ
ἀχθόμενος, καὶ ἐλεύθερος μὴ ἐπαιρόμενος· οὐδεμία γὰρ παρὰ θεῷ διαφορά.Ὁ πιστὸς
δοῦλος οὐδὲν ἔλαττον ἔχει κατὰ τοῦτο τοῦ ἐλευθέρου· παρὰ γὰρ τῷ θεῷ καὶ δοῦλος
ὡς ἐλεύθερος ὁρᾶται καὶ παρ' αὐτῷ ἠλευθέρωται. τοῦτο γὰρ δηλοῖ τὸ ἀπελεύθερος
κυρίου ἐστίν, τοῦτ' ἔστι παρ' αὐτοῦ ἠλευθέρωται τοῦ κυρίου, καὶ ὁ κληθεὶς
ἐλεύθερος εἰς τὴν πίστιν οὐδὲν πλέον ἕξει τοῦ δούλου, ἀλλ' ὁμοίως ἐκείνῳ δοῦλός
ἐστιν Χριστοῦ.Ἀντὶ τοῦ μὴ διὰ τὰς χρείας δουλοπρεπῶς καὶ ἀνελευθέρως διάγετε
θεραπεύοντες ἀνθρώπους, τὸν δὲ ἀληθῆ δεσπότην καταλιμπάνετε, οὗ τῷ αἵματι
ἠγοράσθητε. Οὐκ οἶδεν ἡ χάρις δουλείας καὶ δεσποτείας διαφοράν. μὴ φύγῃς τοίνυν
ὡς ἀναξίαν τῆς πίστεως τὴν δουλείαν· οὐδενὸς γὰρ ἔλαττον ἔχεις τῶν ἐν πίστει διὰ
τοῦτο. εἰ δέ σοι καὶ τοῦ τυχεῖν τῆς ἐλευθερίας εἴη δυνατόν, φροντὶς ἔστω σοι μᾶλλον
ὅπως ἂν εἰς δέον χρήσασθαι δυνηθῇς πλείονα, ὡς ἐν ἐλευθερίᾳ τοῦ κακοῦ τὴν
ἐπιμέλειαν ποιησάμενος. καὶ δεικνὺς ὅτι οὔτε ὁ ἐλεύθερος παρὰ Χριστῷ ἔχει πλέον
διὰ τοῦτο, οὔτε μὴν ὁ δοῦλος ἐλαττοῦται, τούτου γε ἕνεκεν ἐπάγει· ὁ γὰρ ἐν κυρίῳ
κληθεὶς δοῦλος ἀπελεύθερος κυρίου ἐστίν· ὁμοίως ὁ ἐλευθερὸς κληθεὶς δοῦλός ἐστιν
Χριστοῦ. 1 Kor 7,25–26 Πῶς ἐν ἑτέροις λέγων· εἰ δοκιμὴν ζητεῖτε τοῦ ἐν ἐμοὶ
λαλοῦντος Χριστοῦ, νῦν λέγει· ἐπιταγὴν κυρίου οὐκ ἔχω; τίς δ' ἂν δέξαιτο, εἴπερ
λέγει ἃ μὴ ὁ κύριος αὐτῷ ἐπέταξεν; ἀλλὰ δῆλον ὡς οὐ τοῦτο λέγει ὅτι οὐκ ἐπιταγὴν
περὶ παρθενίας διδάξαι, ἀλλ' ὅτι οὐκ ἔλαβεν παρὰ θεοῦ τὸ ἐπιτάξαι ὑμῖν
παρθενεύειν, ἀλλὰ μᾶλλον 252 γνώμην δοῦναι καὶ συμβουλεῦσαι ὡς καλὸν ἡ
παρθενία καὶ χρήσιμον. διὸ καὶ ὡς συμβουλεύων φησὶ νομίζω καὶ καλὸν ὀνομάζει,
καὶ τὴν αἵρεσιν τοῦ αἱρήσασθαι αὐτὴν ἐπὶ τοῖς ἀκούουσι τίθεται. ἀρέσκον δὲ τὸ
πρᾶγμα θεῷ ὡς καὶ ὁ κύριος εἶπεν ὅτι εὐνούχισαν ἑαυτούς τινες διὰ τὴν βασιλείαν,
εὐνουχισμὸν τὴν παρθενίαν καλῶν διὰ τὸ ἀνενέργητον. ἐπιταγὴν οὖν λέγει μὴ
ἔχειν, ἀλλὰ τῇ γνώμῃ συνεχώρησε λέγων· ὁ δυνάμενος χωρεῖν χωρείτω. εἶτα εἰπὼν
ἑαυτὸν πιστόν, ἐμφαίνει ὅτι καὶ πιστὰ λέγει καὶ ἄξια ἐπιτάγματος. τὸ δὲ νομίζω οὐ
διστάζων λέγει ὅτι καλὸν ἡ παρθενία, ἀλλ' ἀσφαλιζόμενος μὴ ἐπίταγμα νομισθῇ. 1
Kor 7,28Ἔδειξεν ὅτι τὴν παρθενίαν εἰσάγει οὐ κατηγορίαν γάμου, ἀλλ' ὅτι διὰ φειδῶ
τῶν ἁγίων εἰσηγεῖται τὴν παρθενίαν, ὡς τὴν σάρκα ὠδίνων καὶ καμάτων
πληροῦντος τοῦ γάμου.Ἔδειξεν ὅτι τὴν παρθενίαν εἰσάγει οὐ κατηγορίαν γάμου,
ἀλλὰ τῶν βιωτικῶν φροντίζων ἀπαλλαγήν. εἶτα εἰπὼν ἐγὼ δὲ ὑμῶν φείδομαι,
φειδῶ τῶν ἁγίων εἰσηγεῖται τὴν παρθενίαν, οὐ κατηγορίαν γάμου. 1 Kor 7,29–
31Ἄλλην αἰτίαν λέγει δι' ἣν προτιμᾷ τὴν παρθενίαν, πανταχοῦ δεικνὺς ὅτι
κατηγορεῖ γάμου τὴν ἁγιωσύνην προτιμῶν· ὅτι πρὸς τῷ τέλει ὁ κόσμος, καὶ δεῖ
εἰδέναι ὅτι ἃ ἔχομεν οὐκ ἔχομεν–ἀφίεμεν γὰρ αὐτά–ἵνα καὶ οἱ ἔχοντες ὡς μὴ
ἔχοντες. εἰ καλόν ἐστι τοῖς ἔχουσιν οὕτως ἔχειν ὡς μὴ ἔχουσιν, πῶς οὐ μᾶλλον τῇ
παρθένῳ μηδὲ προσελθεῖν γάμῳ; καὶ οἱ χρώμενοι τῷ κόσμῳ τούτῳ ὡς μὴ
καταχρώμενοι· τὴν ἄμετρον ἀπόλαυσιν ἐκβάλλει διὰ τούτου, τὴν μέντοι χρείαν
pass_a_gloss: (Continuing: what God) yoked, let man not separate (Matt 19:6). And these also (are) in agreement, the 'and if she is separated, let her remain unmarried', with the things said by the Lord: 'if anyone marries a divorced woman, he commits adultery' (Matt 5:32), and she too if she is married to another. [Label 1 Cor 7:12.] He does not say 'I, not the Lord' as legislating against (the Lord), but because some things the Lord said through himself, but some are said now first by the apostle about the separation of the unbeliever; and he teaches that unbelief does not prevail over faith, but the faith of the one living with (them) sanctifies also the unbeliever. [Label 1 Cor 7:13.] He does not speak of taking an unbeliever, but of putting up with an unbeliever. [Label 1 Cor 7:14.] The children are holy, clean and not defiled even by the unbelief; for over them the faith of the parents prevails rather than the unbelief. [Label 1 Cor 7:17.] To one God apportioned to save, to another to be saved, assigning to each what is worthy of him. And 'to each as God apportioned' he says not (of) having an unbeliever, but (of) putting up with an unbeliever. [Second column, page 251; Label 1 Cor 7:18-24.] Circumcision (is) not good through itself, but because (it was) God's command, and uncircumcision (is) God's creation, not a wage of the uncircumcised. Then he says about the slave: do not be eager about the temporary freedom, but even if you are able, rather use the slavery; for the reward (is) greater, when even occupied about the slavery of men he does not neglect pleasing God. And let each remain in that in which he was called, both a slave not vexed at the slavery, and a free man not lifted up; for (there is) no difference with God. The believing slave has nothing less in this respect than the free; for with God even the slave is seen as free and has been freed by him. For this 'is the Lord's freedman' shows, that is, he has been freed by him, the Lord; and the one called free into the faith will have nothing more than the slave, but likewise with that one is a slave of Christ. Instead of: do not, because of the needs, live slavishly and unfreely serving men, and leave the true Master, by whose blood you were bought. Grace does not know a difference of slavery and mastery. So do not flee the slavery as unworthy of the faith; for you have less than none of those in faith because of this. And if it should be possible for you even to obtain freedom, let your concern rather be how you may be able to use (it) more for what is needed, as having made the care in freedom from evil. And showing that neither does the free (man) have more with Christ because of this, nor indeed is the slave lessened, for this very reason he adds: 'for the one called in the Lord (as) a slave is the Lord's freedman; likewise the one called free is Christ's slave'. [Label 1 Cor 7:25-26.] How, saying in other (places) 'if you seek a proof of Christ speaking in me' (2 Cor 13:3), does he now say 'I do not have a command of the Lord'? Who would accept (him), if he says what the Lord did not command him? But clearly he does not say this, that (he has) not a command to teach about virginity, but that he did not receive from God the commanding you to remain virgins, but rather [page 252] to give an opinion and to advise that virginity (is) good and useful. Therefore also as advising he says 'I think' and names (it) good, and places the choice of choosing it on the hearers. And the thing (is) pleasing to God, as also the Lord said that some made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom (Matt 19:12), calling virginity eunuchhood because of the inactivity. So he says he does not have a command, but allowed (it) to the judgement saying 'the one able to receive, let him receive' (Matt 19:12). Then calling himself trustworthy, he makes evident that he both says trustworthy things and (things) worthy of a command. And 'I think' he says not doubting that virginity (is) good, but making sure it is not thought a command. [Label 1 Cor 7:28.] He showed that he brings in virginity not (as) an accusation of marriage, but that because of sparing the saints he introduces virginity, as marriage filling the flesh with birth-pains and toils. (Unmarked second form:) He showed that he brings in virginity not (as) an accusation of marriage, but caring for release from the things of life. Then saying 'but I spare you', for sparing of the saints he introduces virginity, not (as) an accusation of marriage. [Label 1 Cor 7:29-31.] He says another cause because of which he prefers virginity, everywhere showing that he accuses (as printed; οὐ apparently lost) marriage, preferring holiness: that the world (is) at the end, and one must know that what we have we do not have - for we leave them - so that those having (be) as not having. If it is good for those having to have so as not having, how (is it) not rather (good) for the virgin not even to approach marriage? 'And those using this world as not using (it) up': through this he casts out the unmeasured enjoyment, but the need (… continues in u04-open).
pass_b_english: …has joined together, let no man separate" (Matthew 19:6). These words too, "but if she does separate, let her remain unmarried," agree with what the Lord said: "If anyone marries a woman who has been divorced, he commits adultery" (Matthew 5:32), and so does she, if she is married to another.

On 1 Corinthians 7:12: When he says, "I, not the Lord," he is not laying down a law against the Lord's. Some things the Lord said in person; others, about parting from an unbelieving spouse, are said now for the first time by the apostle. And he teaches that unbelief does not overpower faith; rather, the faith of the believing partner sanctifies even the unbeliever.
On 1 Corinthians 7:13: He is not speaking of taking an unbeliever in marriage, but of bearing with an unbeliever.
On 1 Corinthians 7:14: The children are holy: clean, and not defiled even by the unbelief, for in them the parents' faith wins out over the unbelief.

On 1 Corinthians 7:17: To one God assigned the task of saving, to another that of being saved, giving each what each deserved. By "as God has assigned to each" he does not mean having an unbelieving spouse, but bearing with one.

On 1 Corinthians 7:18–24: Circumcision is not good in itself; it was good because God commanded it. Uncircumcision is God's handiwork, not a reward the uncircumcised have earned. Then he says to the slave: do not set your heart on a freedom that will pass; even if you can gain it, make use of your slavery instead. The reward is greater when a man busy in the service of men does not neglect to please God. Let each one remain in the state in which he was called, the slave not chafing at his slavery, the free man not puffed up, for with God there is no difference.

In this respect a believing slave has nothing less than a free man. With God the slave too is seen as free, and has been set free by him. That is what "is the Lord's freedman" means: he has been freed by the Lord. And the man called to the faith as a free man will have nothing more than the slave; he is Christ's slave just as the other is.
That is: do not, for the sake of your needs, live like slaves, without a free man's spirit, courting men, and so abandon the true Master, whose blood bought you.

Grace knows no difference between slavery and mastery. So do not run from slavery as though it were unworthy of the faith; because of it you have no less than anyone else in the faith. And even if you could obtain your freedom, let your concern be rather how you can make better use of what you have, as one whose care is to be free from evil. To show that the free man has no more with Christ on that account, and that the slave is not made less, he adds, for that very reason: "For he who was called in the Lord as a slave is the Lord's freedman; likewise he who was called as a free man is Christ's slave."

On 1 Corinthians 7:25–26: Elsewhere he says, "since you seek proof of Christ speaking in me" (2 Corinthians 13:3); how then does he now say, "I have no command of the Lord"? Who would accept him if he says what the Lord has not commanded him? Plainly he does not mean that he has no command to teach about virginity. He means that he did not receive from God the right to order you to remain virgins, but rather to give his opinion and advise that virginity is good and useful. That is why, as one giving advice, he says "I think" and calls it "good," and leaves the choice of taking it up to his hearers. The thing is pleasing to God, as the Lord too said that some have made themselves eunuchs for the sake of the kingdom (Matthew 19:12), calling virginity "becoming a eunuch" because the body is left unused. So he says he has no command, and the matter was left to each one's judgment with the words, "Let him who can accept it accept it" (Matthew 19:12). Then, by calling himself trustworthy, he makes plain that what he says is trustworthy and fit to be a command. He says "I think" not because he doubts that virginity is good, but to make sure it is not taken for a command.
On 1 Corinthians 7:28: He showed that he brings in virginity, not to accuse marriage, but to spare the saints; for marriage fills the flesh with birth pains and toil.
The second catena form adds: He is concerned to set them free from the cares of this life, and after saying, "I would spare you," he recommends virginity to spare the saints.

On 1 Corinthians 7:29–31: He gives another reason for preferring virginity, and shows throughout that he does [not] accuse marriage when he prefers holiness. The world is near its end, and we must recognize that what we have we do not really have, since we leave it behind: "so that those who have wives may be as though they had none." If it is good for those who have to have as though they had not, how much better for the virgin not to enter marriage at all? "And those who use this world as though not using it to the full": by this he rules out unmeasured enjoyment, but need…

lemmas.gloss: use to the full, use up

choices.term: Ἔδειξεν ὅτι τὴν παρθενίαν εἰσάγει ... (7:28, twice)
choices.english: collapsed; new material printed after 'The second catena form adds:'
choices.why: Unmarked second form of the 7:28 note; 'out of concern to free them from the cares of this life' and the lemma 'I would spare you' have no counterpart.

choices.english: printed as a normal labelled note
choices.why: The 7:18-24 notes stand in the edition's second column with no first-column counterpart, so there is nothing to collapse.

choices.english: shows throughout that he does [not] accuse marriage
choices.why: As printed the Greek says he accuses marriage, which contradicts the two preceding notes ('not as an accusation of marriage'); a negation appears to have dropped out. The bracketed [not] is a guess and is noted.

choices.term: τῇ γνώμῃ συνεχώρησε λέγων· ὁ δυνάμενος χωρεῖν χωρείτω
choices.english: the matter was left to each one's judgment with the words ...
choices.why: The subject of συνεχώρησε is not stated; the words quoted are the Lord's (Matthew 19:12). A passive avoids naming a subject the Greek leaves open.
Different notes with different lemmas ('the Lord's freedman', 'do not become slaves of men', 'grace knows no difference'), not one note in two forms.

The printed Greek reads ὅτι κατηγορεῖ γάμου ('that he accuses marriage'), against οὐ κατηγορίαν γάμου in the sentence just before and the argument that follows; an οὐ dropped after ὅτι is the likely cause. The supplement is bracketed so the reader sees it.
